system: You are an expert reviewer of machine-learning research ideas.
user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: How much of the zero-shot localisation quality of MVFA (pixel AUROC and Dice on a held-out modality) is retained when its segmentation adapters are trained without pixel masks, using pseudo-masks drawn only from labelled abnormal source images (a patch is anomalous when its frozen CLIP level-4 feature is farther from every normal patch of the same dataset than the 99th percentile of normal-to-normal nearest-neighbour distances on source validation data), as masks are removed from zero, one, or all three masked source datasets?

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Mixing label-restricted pseudo-masks with exact synthetic-lesion masks for mask-free MVFA localisation
SUMMARY: Train MVFA's segmentation adapters on real abnormal images with pseudo-masks plus normal images carrying synthetic lesions with exact masks, and find the mixing ratio that best recovers mask-supervised localisation.
HYPOTHESIS: A mixture with rho between 0.25 and 0.5 recovers at least 90% of the mask-supervised pixel AUROC on held-out masked modalities and beats both pure pseudo-masks (rho = 0) and pure synthesis (rho = 1) by at least 2 pixel-AUROC points.
RESEARCH IDEA: Independent variable: fraction rho of segmentation-branch training samples that are synthetic (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0), with the rest being real abnormal images with label-restricted pseudo-masks (problem rule). Synthetic lesions are created per source dataset from its own images: a random elliptical region (area 0.5-8% of the image) of a normal image is replaced by a Poisson-blended patch cut from an abnormal image's pseudo-anomalous area (so texture is realistic), or by an intensity-perturbed blob (Gaussian intensity shift of +-0.3 x local std) when no anomalous patch exists; the mask is the pasted region. Dependent variables: pixel AUROC and Dice on held-out masked modalities, image AUROC, and the false-positive rate on normal test images at the source-selected threshold.
RATIONALE: Pseudo-masks on real abnormal images have realistic appearance but noisy extents; synthetic lesions pasted into normal images of the same dataset have exact extents but unrealistic appearance. Fed-LoRA shows synthetic abnormal images help few-shot anomaly detection when tailored to the domain. Training the segmentation adapters on a mixture of the two sources should combine their strengths, and the mixing ratio is the key variable.
METHOD: 1) make_pseudo_masks.py: compute label-restricted pseudo-masks for real abnormal source images (problem rule). 2) synth.py: function synth_lesion(normal_img, donor_img, donor_mask) using cv2.seamlessClone (Poisson) with an elliptical mask; fallback blob perturbation. 3) dataset/medical_zero.py: a MixedSegDataset that, per iteration, draws a synthetic sample with probability rho, else a real abnormal sample with pseudo-mask (normal images also drawn as in MVFA). 4) train_zero.py: unchanged losses (Focal + Dice on seg branch, BCE on det branch); synthetic images labelled abnormal for the det branch. 5) Select rho and checkpoint on source-validation pixel AUROC against pseudo-masks (no target data). Hyper-parameters as MVFA (lr 1e-3, 50 epochs, 240 px).
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); pixel metrics on the masked targets BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC. Checkpoints and all thresholds selected on source-modality validation splits only; MVFA re-run under the same rule as the mask-supervised reference; 3 seeds, mean and std. Conditions: rho in {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}; reference with true masks. Ablation: Poisson-blended real texture vs intensity blobs only. Metrics: pixel AUROC, Dice, image AUROC, normal-image FPR. Falsified if no intermediate rho beats both extremes by 2 points or if the best mixture recovers less than 80% of the mask-supervised gain.

Idea B:
TITLE: Joint-bilateral upsampling of patch pseudo-masks guided by the raw image
SUMMARY: Replace superpixel majority voting with a guided (joint-bilateral) filter that upsamples the 17x17 patch pseudo-mask score to 240 px using the raw image as the edge guide, then threshold.
HYPOTHESIS: Guided-filter upsampling of the continuous patch pseudo-mask score raises pseudo-mask Dice against true masks by at least 8 points over nearest-neighbour upsampled patch pseudo-masks, at least as much as SLIC snapping, and MVFA trained on the guided masks reaches at least 90% of the mask-supervised pixel AUROC on held-out masked modalities.
RATIONALE: The parent's goal, putting pseudo-mask boundaries on image edges, is kept; the technique changes. SLIC majority voting makes a hard decision per superpixel and depends on n_segments, which interacts with lesion size and fails when a superpixel straddles the boundary. Joint-bilateral upsampling (the guided filter of He et al.) is the standard technique for upsampling a low-resolution map under a high-resolution guide: it transfers the guide's edges to the map while preserving the map's values, works on continuous scores (so the threshold is applied after refinement), and has two interpretable parameters (radius, epsilon). It therefore addresses the same verified cause, the 14-pixel patch grid at 240 px, with fewer discrete artefacts.
METHOD: 1) make_pseudo_masks.py: continuous score per patch u_p = (d_p - t_95)/(t_99 - t_95) clipped to [0, 1] (label-restricted rule, source-validation percentiles). 2) Bilinear upsampling of u to 240 px. 3) cv2.ximgproc.guidedFilter(guide = normalised raw image, src = upsampled u, radius = 8, eps = 1e-3) (or a 20-line PyTorch box-filter implementation). 4) Mask = refined u > 0.5 on abnormal images; normal images empty. 5) dataset/medical_zero.py loads masks; train_zero.py unchanged (Focal + Dice). 6) radius in {4, 8, 16} and eps in {1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2} selected on source validation where source masks exist. MVFA hyper-parameters otherwise.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); pixel metrics on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC; checkpoints and thresholds selected on source validation only; mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule; 3 seeds, mean and std. Conditions: true masks; nearest-neighbour patch pseudo-masks; SLIC-snapped (parent); guided-filter refined. Masks removed from 1 and 3 masked sources. Metrics: pseudo-mask Dice, boundary F1, trained pixel AUROC, Dice, image AUROC. Falsified if the guided filter does not raise pseudo-mask Dice by 8 points over nearest-neighbour masks or is worse than SLIC snapping.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>

CONFIDENCE: HIGH
